props.title: The Great Gatsby
props.initialSlug: Lavish drama of obsession, wealth, and lost love

sections.content: Jack Clayton's The Great Gatsby stands as a lavish yet complicated adaptation of Fitzgerald's masterpiece, with Robert Redford embodying Jay Gatsby's practiced charm and underlying desperation. The film captures the decadent excess of the 1920s through Douglas Slocombe's dreamy cinematography and Theoni V. Aldredge's Oscar-winning costumes. This version follows several attempts to bring Gatsby to screen, including the lost 1926 silent film and The Great Gatsby with Alan Ladd. Compared to Baz Luhrmann's frenetic The Great Gatsby, Clayton's take maintains a melancholic restraint that better serves the source material's critique of wealth and status.

sections.content: The 1974 Gatsby fits within a broader 1970s fascination with period dramas examining American wealth and power. Films like Chinatown (1974) and The Godfather Part II (1974) used historical settings to comment on contemporary corruption and excess. Robert Evans' production emphasized authenticity in recreating the Jazz Age, from the Newport mansions to the vintage cars. However, some critics found Francis Ford Coppola's screenplay oddly lifeless, failing to capture Fitzgerald's prose despite lifting dialogue directly from the novel.

Mia Farrow's portrayal of Daisy Buchanan remains controversial - her affected performance highlighting the character's superficiality but perhaps missing deeper nuances. The film's pacing draws criticism for being too reverential and staid, especially compared to other literary adaptations of the era like Murder on the Orient Express (1974) or The Day of the Locust (1975). Yet the film's visual grandeur and Redford's star power helped establish a template for how Hollywood approaches prestige literary adaptations. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: Clayton's Gatsby influenced later films about American wealth and social climbing, from Wall Street (1987) to The Wolf of Wall Street (2013). Its attention to period detail and emphasis on the corrupting influence of money resonates through works like There Will Be Blood (2007) and The House of Gucci (2021). The film's portrayal of Gatsby's mansion parties set standards for depicting Jazz Age excess that later adaptations either embraced or deliberately subverted.
